item.title: Government websites restarting after emergency shutdowns
item.description:
Government websites restarting after emergency shutdowns

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Websites in the Netherlands are coming back online following emergency shutdowns. This follows the discovery of vulnerabilities in the programming language on which many government, hospital and news sites are built, including Dutch News.

The organisation behind PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages, said on Tuesday it would patch two flaws in its code.

The announcement prompted hackers to search for the holes and begin trying to attack sites, which US cyber security firm Cloudflare said on Wednesday it was noticing and defending against.

Sites were then swiftly taken down, including the government’s digital ID system DigiD and its online services portal MijnOverheid, the website of parliament, the umbrella organisation for the water boards, and a tool used by local councils for storing documents and scheduling meetings.

Disruptions
Dutch media companies were hit – RTL’s news website and app went down, and broadcaster NPO shut down the system used to upload content to its streaming services.

Several hospitals also took their websites down, as well as charities such as KWF cancer fund and the Dutch Heart Foundation.

Schiphol airport’s app stopped showing live flight information, and benefits agency UWV took a tool people use to report sick or recovered offline.

The problem was not limited to the Netherlands – the Flemish, German, French and Finnish governments all took websites offline.

What happened
Two critical flaws in PHP’s programming language were discovered in August using AI models from OpenAI and Google.

Google-owned cybersecurity firm Wiz, one of the firms that reported the flaws to PHP, said that the vulnerabilities in PHP had existed for over a decade, and said they ranked “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.

PHP built fixes for the vulnerabilities into an update and said all companies using its code should install the update immediately. Prime minister Rob Jetten reiterated this call on social media.

Justice minister David van Weel said the fact that so many websites had been taken offline as a precaution “has an impact on our digital society”.

“Fortunately, there are currently no indications that the vulnerabilities are being actively exploited,” Van Weel stated through his spokesperson.

The National Cyber Security Centre said it had not seen any active hacks, and the PHP Foundation told news agency ANP it also had no indication of breaches.

item.title: Dutch workers more likely to stay on after state retirement age
item.description:
Dutch workers more likely to stay on after state retirement age

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of Dutch workers who stay in work beyond the statutory retirement age has increased by more 50% in eight years, according to latest figures from the statistics agency CBS.

In the second quarter of this year 152,000 people in work were over the age of 67, representing 1.7% of the working population.

In the first quarter of 2018 1.2% of workers were beyond the retirement age, which was then 66, equivalent to 96,000 people.

Men are more likely than women to keep going to work after drawing their pension, the figures show. In June 2.3% of men over 67 were working, compared to 1.1% of women.

The figures also revealed large differences between sectors, with 4.3% of people working in real estate after their 67th birthday compared to 0.6% of civil servants.

A study by the demographic institute NIDI in 2023 found that most people who kept working in retirement did so because they enjoyed their job or to feel useful. Just 10% said the need to earn money was a significant factor.

The Netherlands has the latest retirement age in the European Union, along with Denmark, Sweden, Italy and Greece. The state pension age is due to increase to 67 years and three months in 2028.

item.title: Minister refuses inquiry into abuse at youth home in Spain
item.description:
Minister refuses inquiry into abuse at youth home in Spain

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Long-term care minister Mirjan Sterk has refused to launch an independent investigation into a Dutch youth care scheme in which children are sent abroad, despite revelations about exploitation and harsh treatment.

An investigation by news programme Nieuwsuur found that the “family home” in the Valencia region, which has been running for over 20 years, subjected children living there to cruel physical and psychological punishments.

Sending troubled teenagers abroad is a long-standing practice in Dutch youth care, meant to remove them from difficult environments in the Netherlands. Huize Soria alone received tens of millions of euros in taxpayers’ money over 20 years, according to the investigation.

Reporters found that the Dutch owners of Huize Soria, the Valencia institution, were forcing children their to work long hours. When they misbehaved, they were deprived of food, sleep and access to a toilet.

Some were made to stand stress positions for long periods, others said. Contact with relatives in the Netherlands was restricted, sometimes for months at a time.

Experts described the conditions as “torture”. Huize Soria was ordered to close down in September after evidence of abuse was first uncovered.

Sterk, from the centrist Christian Democrat CDA, has urged youth care organisations to stop placing Dutch children abroad where possible said there was no need for her to order an investigation.

In a letter to parliament, she said it was up to local councils, child protection agencies and care providers who placed the children to make sure the home met the rules.

She also said she did not know which organisations had sent children to Huize Soria, apart from one child protection agency, because there is no central record.

MPs from across the political spectrum said that was exactly why an investigation was needed. Far-right JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie said refusing one was “running away from your responsibilities”.

item.title: Nearly half of Dutch MPs use AI to write speeches in parliament
item.description:
Nearly half of Dutch MPs use AI to write speeches in parliament

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Nearly half of Dutch MPs used artificial intelligence to help write speeches and statements delivered in parliament, according to an investigation based on the AI detection tool Pangram.

A scan of debates and committee hearings revealed that 68 of the 150 MPs from across the political spectrum used AI at least once. Most of the members admitted using artificial intelligence tools when asked by De Groene Amsterdammer and investigations website Investico.

The real number is likely to be higher because only contributions that were found to be more than 50% AI generated were included in the results.

Top of the list was former Pro MP Esmah Lahlah, who is now a member of Amsterdam city council’s executive after leaving parliament in June. The analysis found evidence of AI in her contributions to four debates on poverty and the law on jobseekers.

Lahlah said she sometimes used AI to summarise conversations she had with people during working visits. “Sometimes it was hard to condense those stories into a few minutes’ speaking time, so I used AI,” she said.

Most MPs wrote their own material for big set-piece debates such as the recent debate on the king’s speech, known as the Algemene Politieke Beschouwingen, which kicks off the parliamentary year. But more than half of contributions to committee hearings showed evidence of AI use, the analysis found.

“Rolled out by Chat”

Other frequent users included Rachel van Meetelen of the far-right PVV, who said she used it to make her statements more concise and effective. “I would never say anything in Parliament I didn’t support,” she said.

The heaviest users were right-wing parties such as Gidi Markuszower’s DNA group of former PVV MPs. Only the Socialists (SP), the animal rights party PvdD and Volt showed no use of AI at all.

Harmen Krul of the centre-right CDA also said he used AI to edit his speeches, but not generate content. “I would be dismayed if this created the impression that my contributions were rolled out by Chat,” he said.

Last month an analysis of 28,000 questions in parliament by national broadcaster NOS, again using Pangram, found that around a quarter showed stylistic features of AI.

Prime minister Rob Jetten also had to admit that he used AI to write social media posts, including personal reflections on sensitive subjects such as the mistreatment of Moluccan war veterans who came to the Netherlands in the 1950s.

He defended the practice at the time, saying: “Like three-quarters of Dutch people I sometimes use AI to make things better.”

Some MPs also dismissed the concerns raised by the latest analysis. Henk Vermeer, leader of the farmers’ party BBB, said AI was useful for small parties, after Pangram detected traces in 30% of speeches by his three MPs. “We also use calculators, mobile phones and even coffee makers,” he said.

item.title: Man arrested over discovery of woman’s remains in suitcase
item.description:
Man arrested over discovery of woman’s remains in suitcase

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 23-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the discovery of a woman’s body in a suitcase in Amsterdam.

The victim, 29-year-old Hajar, went missing on October 4 after she was seen cycling away from the Rai area towards Buitenveldert on a bicycle with an unknown man.

Her remains were found on Saturday in a suitcase that had been dumped in the Amsteldijk. The discovery was made nearly two weeks after she disappeared and two days after police issued an appeal for information about her whereabouts.

The suspect, a Somali national of no fixed abode, was arrested on Monday evening in connection with an assault on another man in Koggeland, Noord-Holland.

According to Dutch media reports the victim of the assault was the man’s foster father, who needed hospital treatment for injuries. The suspect had lived in foster care until he was 16 years old.

He had earlier been questioned as a witness about Hajar’s disappearance after camera footage showed him with her at the Rai on October 4.

“Further inquiries led to him being identified as a suspect,” René Beukelaer, head of the prosecution service in Amsterdam told a press conference on Tuesday.

Murder of Lisa

City mayor Femke Halsema acknowledged that the death of Hajar would revive questions about women’s safety, following the murder of a 17-year-old girl, Lisa, on a cycle path in August last year. A 22-year-old asylum seeker, Chris Jude, believed to be from Nigeria, has since admitted killing her.

“It is just 14 months since the Amsterdam authorities had to inquire about the dreadful murder of a 17-year-old girl,” Halsema said.

“The fear, anger and outrage that it stirred up in our society have not been quelled, and it pains me hugely to have to sit here again, knowing that this will cause more fear for women in this city and across the Netherlands.”

Peter Holla, Amsterdam’s chief of police, said the suspect was initially treated as a witness because “there were no signs in the camera footage that he was a suspect or there was a threatening situation.”

Outstanding questions

He said police were still appealing for information from the public to answer outstanding questions, such as where Hajar was killed.

The suspect has lived in the Netherlands since the age of six and has permanent residency. He is being held in solitary detention, with contact restricted to his lawyer.

Beukelaer added there was no indication that the suspect and Hajar knew each other.

Holla said Hajar was reported missing by a family member on October 4 who said she had left home with a suitcase. The search was classed as “urgent” the following day.

Public appeal

“It was not clear at that time whether we were dealing with a crime,” Holla said.

Her photograph was circulated to the public on October 13, along with details of when she was last seen at Rai.

The family told police Hajar had spent periods of time away from home before, but always returned, Holla said.

At the start of the press conference, Halsema extended her sympathies to Hajar’s family and close friends.

“For nearly two weeks they lived between hope and fear,” she said. “A few days ago the worst possible scenario was confirmed: the 29-year-old Hajar had been violently deprived of her life.

“I ask everyone to respect the peace and anonymity of the family.”

item.title: PSV hold on to book narrow Champions League win in Porto
item.description:
PSV hold on to book narrow Champions League win in Porto

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

PSV survived a second-half onslaught in Porto to secure their first win of the Champions League group stages.

Guus Til scored the only goal when he tapped in from close range after Esmir Bajraktarevic’s shot had come back off the post and was steered across goal by Sven Mijnans.

The Eindhoven club were worth their narrow lead against Francesco Farioli’s side after dominating possession in the first half, but rarely troubled Diogo Costa in the Porto goal.

Til went close with a header early in the second half before putting PSV ahead in the 57th minute.

But the visitors had to defend heroically as Porto poured forward in search of an equaliser, aided by an increasingly fragile Matej Kovar.

The goalkeeper put his defenders in jeopardy with a weak clearance in the 72nd minute, but redeemed himself by saving Victor Froholdt’s shot with his chest before Lutsarel Geertruida blocked the follow-up from Pepê.

A minute later Kovar was left stranded after he rushed out of his penalty area, but Sergiño Dest managed to hack the ball away before Alberto Costa could poke it into the open goal.

At the other end, substitute Denis Man came close to scoring a second for PSV with his first touch when his curling shot beat Costa but failed to sneak inside the post.

The 1-0 win lifts PSV to a provisional 16th place in the Champions League table at the halfway stage of round three, while Porto are still looking for their first point.

Their next match is at home to Belgian side Club Brugge, who will make the short trip to Eindhoven on November 4.

item.title: Churches offer refugees temporary shelter to free up asylum beds
item.description:
Churches offer refugees temporary shelter to free up asylum beds

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Council of Churches in the Netherlands is temporarily stepping in to help shelter refugees amid the ongoing asylum crisis.

An overflow of asylum seekers continues to leave many sleeping outside, while those who have already been given residence permits stay in asylum centres awaiting housing.

This caused trouble throughout the summer months, and, with winter approaching, the shortage of beds poses a new danger to the homeless.

The initiative, called Actie Onderdak, was launched by the Council’s 19 member churches and organisations, including protestant, catholic and reformed denominations.

The Council has written to all local councils and parishes asking them to help shelter families currently housed in asylum centres so more beds can be freed up.

The Council requested churches offer space in empty rectories or annexes where possible. The intention is to give families three months in a new location where they can “find peace and get to know their surroundings”.

The plan was developed in coordination with the refugee settlement agency COA, and also endorsed by asylum minister Bart van den Brink.

According to the Council, COA will ensure refugees can move on to a new location after their three-month church stay ends.

item.title: Dutch winter gas storage levels reach minimum limit of 64%
item.description:
Dutch winter gas storage levels reach minimum limit of 64%

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands has met its target for filling its gas reserves before the onset of winter, but only after reducing its limit to the European Union minimum of 64%.

The Dutch government set a target of 80% capacity by November 1 in 2022, after the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine sent wholesale prices soaring.

Last year it only managed to reach 73.6%, while a surge in prices triggered by the United States’ military action against Iran prompted the state energy company EBN, which is responsible for buying winter supplies, to reduce its orders.

In August the reserves were 45% full, prompting EBN to ask the government to lower its target to 64%, the minimum level agreed between EU member states.

Since then the reserves have been filled to 65.5% and the company hopes to be able to keep topping up supplies for another two weeks.

Last year the level peaked on November 1 and began falling on November 7. At the lowest point, on April 2, the reserves were just 4.5% full.

item.title: Amsterdam hopes 20km/h cycle lane limit will change behaviour
item.description:
Amsterdam hopes 20km/h cycle lane limit will change behaviour

October 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam city council has introduced an experimental speed limit of 20km/h for cyclists to see if riders can be persuaded to slow down.

Tourists, commuters and shoppers have all complained in recent years of feeling unsafe on the capital’s congested bike paths, but the only speed restriction is a 30 km/h limit for motor vehicles.

A temporary speed limit has been set on a section of Amstelveenseweg, one of the main routes into the city from the south, for four weeks to gauge its effect on cyclists’ behaviour.

But instead of enforcing the limit through fines and cautions, the city council has put up boards showing people how many of their fellow bike users are staying below 20 km/h, in the hope they will nudge people into being more considerate.

Traffic alderman Elise Moeskops told AT5 the idea of the experiment is to see if the signs will encourage a shift in cycling culture.

“If you enforce everything in the city you end up with a very harsh police state, and we don’t have the staff for that,” she said.

Infrastructure problems

“Are people prepared to cycle more slowly if we remind them that that’s an option? The question is what the social norm is on the cycle lane, because we don’t really know.”

But Kees Bakker, spokesman for the cyclists’ union Fietsersbond, was sceptical of the idea. He said better infrastructure was the solution to crowded bike lanes.

“The cycle lane on that road is very narrow and poorly laid out,” he told Dutch News. “There’s a busy pavement alongside it, so pedestrians spill over to the cycle path.

“It doesn’t make much difference if the speed limit is 20 km/h or 50 km/h, because the path is too narrow and there’s no room to overtake.”

Bakker said speed limits were likely to be less effective in bike lanes because not all cyclists travel at the same speed and they need space to overtake.

“Cars mostly drive in file at 30 km/h, but the range of speeds is much wider for cyclists,” he said. “Some of them ride at 15 km/h, others do 25 or even 30. There needs to be room to accommodate everyone, including people who want to coast along side by side at 15 km/h.”

item.title: Dutch destinations: Go back in time in eastern Drenthe
item.description:
Dutch destinations: Go back in time in eastern Drenthe

October 20, 2026 Robin Pascoe

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eastern Drenthe is perhaps the most underrated part of the Netherlands. Its rolling scenery, its history and its villages – low thatched farmhouses, tiny brick churches and woodlands – make it a perfect place to spend a few sunny autumn days.

Assen is the provincial capital. It has the region’s main museum and boasts the second-biggest department store in the Netherlands. It is also home to the Dutch TT circuit, offering a wide variety of motorcycle races from April to October. But the real charm of the region is in the countryside.

A weekend is not enough to take in everything, so here is a taster of what eastern Drenthe has to offer.

What to do

Visit the hunebedden
Eastern Drenthe is all about hunebedden, the Neolithic burial chambers built by the Funnel Beaker people over 5,000 years ago. Drenthe is home to 52 of the 54 known hunebedden in the Netherlands, and many are concentrated around Borger, where the national hunebed centre is based.

The biggest hunebed, with the not-so-romantic name D27, is located in the woods next to the visitors’ centre. The grounds are also home to a bizarre collection of zwerfstenen, or boulders, which were brought down to the province from Scandinavia by glaciers. Many of the stones have labels showing exactly where in Sweden or Norway they came from.

In addition, the centre has a café and a sort of Neolithic playground – the Prehistoric Park – where children can check out recreations of ancient homes. During peak season volunteers in costume are on hand to explain about the lives of people who lived in the region and demonstrate ancient crafts. No dogs.

Walk along the Hondsrug
The Hondsrug (literally “dog’s back”) is listed as a Unesco Global Geopark because of its unique history, deriving from the last two ice ages. This 70-kilometre-long glacial ridge made of sand and clay is the only one of its kind in Europe. There are dozens of walking and cycle trails to explore, as well as small museums, such as the De Nabershof working farm near Emmen. You can find out more about the region’s geology at the visitors centre, next to the hunebed centre in Borger.

Stroll around Orvelte
About 20 minutes south of Assen is Orvelte, a Drenthe village untouched by time, which has become a sort of open-air museum. It’s car-free – you park on the outskirts – but there is a horse-drawn “bus” if you have little ones with you who don’t want to walk.

Stroll past the thatched farmhouses, stop off for what we were told is the best apple pie in Drenthe, and check out the little museums – which seem to be based largely on the locals’ hobbies, such as collecting model cars and rare sheep.

There is a good sprinkling of shops, some of which sell tourist tat, but some are upmarket outlets selling wonderful antique pottery and glass, as well as clothes and bric-a-brac. Plenty of options for lunch and morning coffee. If you are into Christmas themes, Orvelte will transform into a Christmas village from December 18 to 20.

Catch up on history at the Drents Museum in Assen
The Drents Museum in the provincial capital Assen hit the headlines in 2025 when criminals broke in overnight and stole a number of priceless gold relics, most of which have since been recovered. There is no Romanian gold on show any longer – the current special exhibition is about Angkor in Cambodia – but the museum is well worth a visit to find out more about the history of the region.

It is heavy on the infotainment, so there’s plenty to keep the kids occupied, but the museum nevertheless has something for everyone. Located in several buildings linked by tunnels and overground walkways, the museum has Neolithic finds, art (a couple of Van Goghs), recreated stijlkamers (period rooms), temporary exhibitions and a fine café for lunch.

Go on a tree walk
The Boomkroonpad – treetop path – takes you from the roots of an oak tree up into the treetops, where you can walk along a very solid metal structure and admire the forest from above. The path is also the starting point for five forest floor walks, ranging from three to 16.5 kilometres, and there are plenty of organised activities for families – deer and mushroom spotting, for example – all year round.

Where to eat
All the attractions we visited had cafés for lunch, mainly selling standard-fare sandwiches and broodjes kroket. Assen has a good selection of cafés and restaurants for dinner. We ate at our hotel, Rikus, which uses local produce and offers three-, four- and five-course menus. Be warned: the portions are big as well as being delicious.

Where to stay
Rikus, a small hotel in the village of Eext, about 20 minutes from Assen and Borger, has an eclectic interior and big bedrooms with views over the countryside. As a couple we paid €331 for bed, breakfast, a three-course dinner and drinks.

There is a hotel and a quaint-looking B&B in Orvelte, and Assen is home to Hotel de Jonge, with a large café terrace in the heart of the old city. Drenthe is popular with Dutch holidaymakers, so, as you would expect, there are plenty of campsites and holiday parks to choose from as well.

Anything else
Unless you are big on cycling or long walks, you really need a car to get around the region. The attractions can get very busy at weekends in the summer months, which may well dent their charm. The Dutch TT Grand Prix takes place on the last Sunday in June.
